ap_statistics-m01.stem: A teacher asks students to write a question that requires a statistical investigation. Which of the following questions does so?

options.text: If each of 4 walkers takes 8,000 steps in a day, how many steps do the walkers take altogether?
options.why: It is answered by a fixed calculation with the given numbers, so no data have to be collected and analyzed.

options.text: How much do the daily numbers of steps vary among the adult residents of a city?
options.why: It asks about a variable that takes different values for different individuals in a population, so it is answered by collecting and analyzing data.

options.text: Is a brisk walk a nobler form of exercise than a swim?
options.why: It asks for a moral or aesthetic judgment, which no data on a measured variable can settle.

options.text: How many days are there in a leap year?
options.why: It has a single factual answer that can be looked up, so no variability among individuals is anticipated.

ap_statistics-m02.stem: A researcher wants to estimate the proportion of households with a vegetable garden among the 480 households in a village and has a complete list of the households. The sample size will be $50$. Which of the following plans is most likely to give an estimate that is not biased?

options.text: Post the survey on the village's website and use the answers of the households that choose to respond.
options.why: Volunteers or respondents who choose to reply can differ from the whole population, so the estimate can be biased.

options.text: Survey the first $50$ households that the researcher meets while walking along the main street.
options.why: Selecting the individuals who are easiest to reach leaves out the others and tends to give a biased estimate.

options.text: Number the households on the list from $1$ to $480$, use a random number generator to choose $50$ different numbers, and survey those households.
options.why: Every individual on the complete list has the same chance of being chosen, so the sample tends to represent the whole population.

options.text: Ask the village council to choose $50$ households that it considers typical of the village.
options.why: Selecting individuals that someone considers typical introduces the chooser's judgment and does not give every individual a chance.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Choose the sampling plan that gives every individual a chance and avoids selection bias
student_thinking: Compare how each plan chooses the individuals and who could be left out
Select the plan that uses chance with a complete list and reject plans driven by volunteering, convenience or judgment

options.why: Selecting the individuals who are easiest to reach leaves out the others and tends to give a biased estimate.

options.text: Ask $40$ members whom the club president knows to be frequent hikers.
options.why: Selecting individuals that someone considers typical introduces the chooser's judgment and does not give every individual a chance.

options.text: Send an e-mail to all members and use the first $40$ replies.
options.why: Volunteers or respondents who choose to reply can differ from the whole population, so the estimate can be biased.

options.text: Assign each member a number from the roster, select $40$ different numbers at random, and ask those members.
options.why: Every individual on the complete list has the same chance of being chosen, so the sample tends to represent the whole population.

ap_statistics-m03.stem: To estimate the proportion of adults in the city who own a laptop, a researcher interviews $400$ adults selected at the checkout counters of a computer store. Shoppers at a computer store are more likely to own a laptop than other adults in the city. Which of the following statements about the estimates from this plan is correct?

options.text: There is no bias, because the adults are chosen by chance from those who check out.
options.why: Choosing by chance among the individuals who happen to be available does not remove the bias, because those who are available differ from the whole population.

options.text: The estimates will tend to be too small, because shoppers at a computer store are less likely to own a laptop than other adults in the city, and only those shoppers can be selected.
options.why: Reverses the direction: the stated difference between the sampled group and the population pushes the estimates the other way.

options.text: The estimates will tend to be too large, because shoppers at a computer store are more likely to own a laptop than other adults in the city, and only those shoppers can be selected.
options.why: The sampled individuals are not representative of the population, and the stated difference shows which way the estimates are pushed.

options.text: There is no bias, because a sample of $400$ is large.
options.why: A large sample does not remove bias from a flawed way of selecting individuals; it only makes the biased estimate more precise.

blueprint.concept: Decide the direction of the bias that a flawed way of selecting individuals produces
student_thinking: Compare the people who can be selected with the whole population on the variable being estimated
Use the stated difference to decide whether the estimates are pushed up or down, and reject claims that chance within the available group or a large sample removes bias

ap_statistics-m04.stem: Among the households in a town, $36\%$ have a dog, $40\%$ have a cat, and $11\%$ do both. One is selected at random. What is the probability that the selected one does neither? (Probabilities are given to two decimal places.)

options.why: Adds the overlap instead of subtracting it when finding the probability of at least one event, so the probability of neither comes out too small.
Subtracts the two probabilities from $1$ without adding back the overlap that was counted twice.
Stops at the probability of at least one event and does not take the complement.
The probability of at least one is $0.36 + 0.40 - 0.11 = 0.65$, and the probability of neither is $1 - 0.65 = 0.35$.

ap_statistics-m05.stem: For which of the following is the random variable described a binomial random variable?

options.text: An inspector tests light bulbs chosen at random from a very large shipment in which $4\%$ are defective until the first defective bulb is found, and counts the bulbs tested.
options.why: The number of trials is not fixed in advance; the variable counts trials until the first success.

options.text: An inspector chooses $20$ bulbs one at a time, without replacement, from a box of exactly $24$ bulbs of which $9$ are defective, and counts the defective bulbs.
options.why: The sample is a large part of a small box, so removing a bulb changes the probability for the next one and the trials are not independent.

options.text: A quality inspector tests $20$ light bulbs chosen at random from a very large shipment in which $4\%$ of the bulbs are defective, and counts the defective bulbs.
options.why: The number of trials is fixed, each trial has two outcomes with the same probability, and the trials are independent, so the count of successes is a binomial random variable.

options.text: An inspector tests $20$ bulbs chosen at random from a very large shipment and records the number of hours that each bulb lasts, then reports the mean lifetime.
options.why: The variable is a measured lifetime rather than a count of successes in a fixed number of independent trials with two outcomes.

blueprint.concept: Recognize the conditions that make a count a binomial random variable
student_thinking: Check each description for a fixed number of trials, two outcomes, a constant probability and independence
Keep the description that meets every condition and reject those that count trials to a first success, sample a small group without replacement or measure a quantity

ap_statistics-m05.stem: For which of the following is the random variable described a binomial random variable?

options.text: A coach draws $12$ players one at a time, without replacement, from a team of $24$ players of whom $9$ are starters, and counts the starters drawn.
options.why: Sampling a large part of a small group without replacement makes the probability change from draw to draw.

options.text: A player takes $12$ shots, some from the free-throw line worth $1$ point and some from the three-point line worth $3$ points, and the coach adds the points to get a total score.
options.why: The variable is a total of point values from different kinds of shots rather than a count of successes with two outcomes per trial.

options.text: A basketball player keeps shooting free throws, making each one with probability $0.7$ independently of the others, until she misses, and the coach counts the shots she takes.
options.why: The number of trials is not fixed in advance.

options.text: A basketball player takes $12$ free throws in a practice, making each one with probability $0.7$ independently of the other shots, and the coach counts the number that she makes.
options.why: The number of trials is fixed, each trial has two outcomes with the same probability, and the trials are independent, so the count of successes is a binomial random variable.

options.why: Forgets to add the constant to the mean.

options.text: mean $128$ points, standard deviation $9$ points

options.text: mean $128$ points, standard deviation $21.5$ points

ap_statistics-m07.stem: The true value of the proportion of all voters in a city who support a measure is $0.4$. A researcher compares four estimators by simulating $2000$ samples for each and computing the estimate from every sample. The table shown gives the mean and the standard deviation of the estimates for each estimator. Which estimator is best for estimating the true value?

stimulus.description: Mean and standard deviation of the estimates from 2000 simulated samples

data.title: Results of 2000 simulated samples for each estimator

options.text: Estimator B, because its sampling distribution has the largest spread and so covers the most possible values.
options.why: Treats a larger spread as an advantage; more variability means estimates that are farther from the parameter more often.

options.text: Estimator A, because it has the smallest spread of all the estimators.
options.why: Considers variability alone; the center of this sampling distribution is not at the true value, so the estimator is biased.

options.text: Estimator C, because the center of its sampling distribution is at the true value.
options.why: Considers bias alone; another estimator is also centered at the true value and has less variability.

options.text: Estimator D, because the center of its sampling distribution is at the true value and its spread is the smallest among the estimators that are centered there.
options.why: An estimator that is unbiased has a sampling distribution centered at the parameter, and among unbiased estimators the one with the least variability is best.
